question: What does the Bible say about what is called total depravity?
intro: Christians agree that sin is in every person and that rescue comes from God, and they ask how far sin reaches: whether it leaves the mind, the will and the image of God standing in some measure, and whether anyone can turn to God before God's grace has acted. This page sets the main readings side by side, each in the words its holders use, and chooses none of them. These are Christian readings; Jewish tradition reads the Hebrew Scriptures cited here differently, and does not teach inherited sin.

agreed.summary: Every reading below takes the text to say that all people have sinned, that sin brings death, that salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith, and that God calls people to repent and believe. The readings differ in how far they take sin to have reached the capacities of the person (the mind, the conscience, the will, the image of God), and in whether and how God's grace enables a person to turn to him.

passages.quote: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God,
Surely there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins.
For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God,
Repent and believe in the gospel!

readings.label: Wounded and healed: the fall brought death and disorder to every person, the image of God remains, and grace heals the will and moves it
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the text to say that Adam's sin brought death and a disordered nature to all his descendants, and that human nature is wounded by it and not destroyed: the image of God, the conscience and the freedom of the will remain. Catholic teaching calls the inherited condition original sin, a state contracted by descent and not a personal act, and says that human nature has not been totally corrupted (Catechism 404-405). The Council of Trent teaches that free will was weakened and not extinguished (Session 6, chapter 1 and canon 5), that the first movement toward faith is itself given by grace, which a free will may assent to or refuse (Session 6, chapter 5), and that the view that all works done before justification are sins is to be rejected (Session 6, canon 7). Catholic teaching also holds that the inclination to sin that remains after baptism (what is called concupiscence) is not itself sin (Session 5, canon 5). The Orthodox Church in America, in a reply on its teaching pages, says that the consequences of the first sin, chiefly death, pass to all while only Adam and Eve are guilty of it. The Confession of Dositheus (1672) names what descended from the first man as the punishments that followed his transgression and not personal sins, and says that the fallen person keeps the created power to choose the good while unable of himself to do any work worthy of a Christian life. Orthodox readers speak of God's grace and the human will working together (what is called synergy). The two traditions differ over guilt and share the picture of a person wounded and healed. Some members of other traditions hold parts of this reading.

passages.quote: So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them.
passages.note: Humankind created in God's image, which these readers hold is marred by the fall and not lost.

passages.quote: Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man his blood will be shed; for in His own image God has made mankind.
passages.note: After the flood the image is still named as the reason human life is protected.

passages.quote: With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in God's likeness.
passages.note: Long after the fall, people are still spoken of as made in God's likeness.

passages.quote: For since the creation of the world God's invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship, so that men are without excuse.
passages.note: Read as saying that God can be known from what he has made, a capacity of the mind that remains.

passages.quote: the work of the law is written on their hearts, their consciences also bearing witness
passages.note: Read as naming a conscience that bears witness among those who do not have the law.

passages.quote: A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho when he fell into the hands of robbers. They stripped him, beat him, and went away, leaving him half dead.
passages.note: Early Christian writers read the traveler left half dead allegorically, as humankind wounded by the fall; this is their reading of the parable and not its stated point.

passages.quote: Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so also death was passed on to all men, because all sinned.
passages.note: Sin and death passing from one man to all, which Catholic readers call original sin and Orthodox readers ancestral sin.

passages.quote: For we are God's fellow workers; you are God's field, God's building.
passages.note: Read by Orthodox readers as naming human beings who work together with God.
passages.context_note: The 'we' is named just before: 'What then is Apollos? And what is Paul? They are servants through whom you believed, as the Lord has assigned to each his role.' They are the ones who planted and watered ('I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow'), and 'you' are the Corinthians, God's field.

passages.quote: through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners
passages.note: Through the disobedience of one man the many were made sinners, and through one man's obedience the many will be made righteous.

passages.quote: where sin increased, grace increased all the more
passages.note: Where sin increased, grace increased all the more.

passages.quote: I was sinful when my mother conceived me
passages.note: David says he was sinful from the time his mother conceived him.

passages.quote: we were by nature children of wrath
passages.note: Paul says that 'we', like the rest, were by nature children of wrath.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take the verses that speak of deadness and inability (Romans 3:10-12, Ephesians 2:1, Romans 8:7) to describe the hold of sin on the person and the loss of life with God, while the will and the image are wounded and still present, which is why the text still calls people to turn. They take John 6:44 to describe the Father's drawing, to which a free will answers, and Genesis 6:5 and 8:21 to describe how deep wickedness runs in a generation and in the human heart, with Genesis 9:6 and James 3:9 speaking of the image afterward. They take Psalm 51:5 as the psalmist's confession of the sinfulness he shares with all people, a condition received by descent and not a personal act of his own.

readings.label: Sin reaches every part of the person (what is called total depravity): left to itself no one seeks God or can turn to him, and God's grace gives the new heart
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the text to say that sin has touched every part of a person (the mind, the heart, the will), so that no one, apart from God's work in them, is able to seek God or to believe. “Total” names the reach of sin through the whole person and does not say that anyone is as evil as they could be. In this reading God's grace brings the new heart and faith; Reformed readers place the new birth before faith, and Lutheran readers hold that the Spirit works faith through the Word and sacraments. Reformed readers state it as total depravity or total inability, the first of what are called the five points of Calvinism; their churches state the teaching in the Westminster Confession (held by the Presbyterian Church in America and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church) and in the Canons of Dort (held by the Christian Reformed Church), in their own words. Lutheran readers speak of the bondage of the will in spiritual matters: the will is unable to turn to God and is not forced (Solid Declaration, Article II), and Lutherans differ from Reformed readers over whether grace can be resisted. Baptists of the 1689 London Confession state the same inability in their confession, and other Baptist and free-church readers who stand with the Reformed account hold it; others in those traditions hold the third reading. The Church of England's Articles IX and X say that human nature is far gone from original righteousness and that no one can turn and prepare himself by his own strength; Anglican members hold the reading in part, and they differ among themselves.

passages.quote: every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was altogether evil all the time.
passages.note: Cited by these readers for how deep evil runs in the heart; the verse describes the generation before the flood.

passages.quote: Surely I was brought forth in iniquity; I was sinful when my mother conceived me.
passages.note: Cited by these readers as the psalmist's confession of a sin present from conception; the verse is part of a prayer of confession.

passages.quote: All of us also lived among them at one time, fulfilling the cravings of our flesh and indulging its desires and thoughts. Like the rest, we were by nature children of wrath.
passages.note: Read as naming a condition belonging to people by nature, apart from their own acts.

passages.quote: There is no one who understands, no one who seeks God.
passages.note: Part of Paul's chain of quotations from the Psalms (Romans 3:10-12): no one seeks God.

passages.quote: the mind of the flesh is hostile to God: It does not submit to God's law, nor can it do so.
passages.note: The mind of the flesh named as unable to submit to God.

passages.quote: And you were dead in your trespasses and sins,
passages.note: Read as spiritually lifeless and unable to respond until made alive (Ephesians 2:5).

passages.quote: The natural man does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God. For they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned.
passages.note: The natural man named as unable to understand the things of the Spirit.

passages.quote: No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him, and I will raise him up at the last day.
passages.note: Coming to Christ tied to the Father's drawing.

passages.quote: The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure.
passages.note: The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure.

passages.quote: death was passed on to all men, because all sinned
passages.note: Sin entered the world through one man, and death spread to all men.

passages.quote: no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again
passages.note: Jesus says that no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again.

passages.quote: every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth
passages.note: The LORD says that every inclination of man's heart is evil from his youth.

passages.quote: all our righteous acts are like filthy rags
passages.note: The prayer of Israel's confession: all our righteous acts are like filthy rags.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take the verses on the image of God (Genesis 1:27, 9:6, James 3:9) to name a dignity that persists while the image is marred in the person's love for God, and take Romans 2:14-15 to describe a conscience and a knowledge of right that remain without the power to please God (Romans 8:8). They read Romans 5:12-19 with Ephesians 2:3 as naming a condition passed from Adam to all. They take the calls to turn (Acts 17:30, Deuteronomy 30:19, Isaiah 55:6) to name the duty of the hearer, and read the promises of a new heart (Deuteronomy 30:6, Ezekiel 36:26) as the way God gives it. Reformed readers take Titus 2:11 and John 12:32 to speak of people from every nation, or of grace offered in the preaching, and not of an inner drawing given to each person. Lutheran readers take Titus 2:11 and John 12:32 of God's grace toward every person, and hold that the lost are lost by their own rejection (Solid Declaration, Article XI).

readings.label: Grace that goes before (what is called prevenient grace): sin has left no one able to turn to God unaided, and God's grace given to everyone makes a free response possible
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the text to say that sin has reached the whole person and left no one able to turn to God by their own power, and also that God's grace goes before every person and restores enough freedom to answer his call or to refuse it. Wesleyan and Methodist readers call this prevenient grace and place it as the first work of grace in a way of salvation that continues through justification and holiness; the Articles of Religion of the United Methodist Church (Article VIII) say that no one can do good works pleasing to God without the grace of God by Christ preventing us, and Wesley's sermons say that grace of this kind is given to every person. The Assemblies of God uses the term in its position paper on assurance. Many Baptist and free-church readers, other Pentecostal and Charismatic readers, and Anabaptist readers hold a similar account without always using the term. The 1995 Mennonite confession says that sinfulness affects the whole person and that people's own efforts alone are constantly corrupted, and also that God saves without coercion; Anabaptist readers speak of a call that grace makes possible to answer, and put weight on the response of discipleship. Members of each of these traditions differ among themselves, and some hold the second reading. Catholic members hold the grace that goes before in part, as Trent and the Catechism teach it, and place it with the first reading. Eastern Orthodox members hold the grace that goes before in part, as the Confession of Dositheus (1672) speaks of a preventing grace imparted to all and of use to those who are willing to cooperate with it, and place it with the first reading. Anglican members hold parts of this reading and parts of the second; Article X of the Church of England speaks of grace preventing us.

passages.quote: The true Light, who gives light to everyone, was coming into the world.
passages.note: The light is said to give light to everyone.

passages.quote: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone.
passages.note: Grace bringing salvation to everyone.

passages.quote: And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself.
passages.note: Read together with John 6:44: the drawing is said to reach everyone.

passages.quote: Or do you disregard the riches of His kindness, tolerance, and patience, not realizing that God's kindness leads you to repentance?
passages.note: God's kindness named as what leads to repentance.

passages.quote: Although God overlooked the ignorance of earlier times, He now commands all people everywhere to repent.
passages.note: All people everywhere commanded to repent.

passages.quote: I call heaven and earth as witnesses against you today that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life, so that you and your descendants may live,
passages.note: Life and death set before the people, with a call to choose.

passages.quote: Seek the LORD while He may be found; call on Him while He is near.
passages.note: A call to seek, read as addressed to people whom grace enables to answer.

passages.quote: For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose.
passages.note: God named as the one who works the willing as well as the acting.

passages.quote: No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him
passages.note: No one comes to Jesus unless the Father who sent him draws him.

passages.quote: you were dead in your trespasses and sins
passages.note: Paul tells his readers they were dead in their trespasses and sins.

passages.quote: There is no one who understands, no one who seeks God.
passages.note: No one understands and no one seeks God.

passages.quote: who wants everyone to be saved
passages.note: God wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take the verses on inability and deadness (Romans 3:11, Ephesians 2:1, 1 Corinthians 2:14, John 6:44) to describe a person apart from God's grace, which they take to have been given to all, so that no one remains in that condition. They read John 6:44 with John 12:32, and Romans 9:16 and Philippians 2:13 as saying that the will's turning rests on God's work and not on an effort that earns it. They take Genesis 6:5 and Jeremiah 17:9 to describe the human heart in sin, and the calls and promises of Deuteronomy 30 and Isaiah 55 as offers that grace lets people accept. They take Psalm 51:5 as the psalmist's words about his own sin and the sin all people share.

terms.note: Reformed churches state this teaching in the Westminster Confession (6.2-6.4, 9.3), held by the Presbyterian Church in America and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church, and in the Canons of Dort (Third and Fourth Heads), held by the Christian Reformed Church, in their own words. The label total depravity, the first of what are called the five points of Calvinism, is later shorthand for the Canons' teaching and is not the phrase of either text. “Total” names the reach of sin and not that each person is as evil as possible.
The Lutheran and Reformed phrase for the will's inability to turn itself toward God; Lutheran and Reformed readers differ in what follows from it.

The Western term for the sin and its effects passing from Adam to his descendants. Catholic teaching calls it a state contracted and not committed; Lutheran and Reformed readers speak of inherited corruption and guilt; traditions differ over whether guilt is inherited. The term is not in the Bible; it names a reading of Romans 5:12 and related verses that Christians have held in various forms since the early church.

A term that Eastern Orthodox writers often use in place of original sin for what is passed on from Adam. None of the Orthodox documents cited on this card uses it; the Orthodox Church in America page speaks of the first sin and says its consequences, chiefly death, pass to all while only Adam and Eve are guilty of it.

The Catholic term for the inclination to sin that remains after baptism; Catholic teaching holds that it is not itself sin (Council of Trent, Session 5, canon 5). Article IX of the Church of England holds that it has of itself the nature of sin even in the baptized, and the Lutheran Apology (Article II) and the Westminster Confession (6.5) also call it sin.
The Eastern Orthodox term for the human will working together with God's grace.
The Wesleyan and Methodist term for God's grace that comes before and enables a person's response; other traditions use other words for the grace that goes before faith.

New birth. Reformed readers place it before faith and as its cause; Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran readers connect it with baptism; Wesleyan readers place it at the new birth that comes with justifying faith, and the Methodist Articles of Religion call baptism its sign (Article XVII); Baptist and other readers differ in where they place it.
The Berean's rendering in 1 Corinthians 2:14; traditions and scholars differ over whether it names every person apart from the Spirit's work, or the person who relies on human wisdom.

further_reading.title: Council of Trent, Session 5, Decree on Original Sin, canons 1-5
further_reading.says: It teaches that Adam's sin harmed his descendants as well as himself, that the guilt of original sin is remitted in baptism, and that the inclination to sin that remains (concupiscence) does not harm those who refuse consent and resist by Christ's grace.

further_reading.title: Council of Trent, Session 6, Decree on Justification, chapters 1 and 5 and canons 1, 3-5 and 7
further_reading.says: It teaches that free will was weakened and not extinguished by Adam's sin, that the beginning of justification comes from God's grace that goes before, to which the will may freely assent, and it condemns the view that all works done before justification are sins (canon 7).

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 396-409 (The Fall: Original Sin)
further_reading.says: It teaches that original sin is contracted and not committed, a state passed on by descent, and that human nature has not been totally corrupted but is wounded in its natural powers and inclined to sin (404-405).

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1996-2005 (Grace and Justification: Grace)
further_reading.says: It teaches that the human preparation to receive grace is itself a work of grace, and that God's free initiative calls for a free human answer (2001-2002).

further_reading.title: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem, 1672), Decrees 3, 6 and 14
further_reading.says: Decree 3 speaks of a preventing grace imparted to all and of use to the willing; Decree 6 says hereditary sin passed from the first man to his posterity and names the punishments that followed his transgression, and not personal sins, as what descended; Decree 14 says the fallen person is able by nature to choose the good and not able of himself to do any work worthy of a Christian life.

further_reading.title: The Longer Catechism of Philaret of Moscow, questions 162-169
further_reading.says: It teaches that God gave man a will inclined to love him yet free, that man used it for evil and so brought death, and that all who come of Adam are infected by sin and mortal, and all sin themselves, as an infected source passes its condition to the stream (Romans 5:12).

further_reading.title: Augsburg Confession, Article II (Of Original Sin)
further_reading.says: It teaches that people born after Adam's fall come into the world without the fear of God and without trust in God, and with concupiscence, which it calls truly sin.

further_reading.title: Apology of the Augsburg Confession, Article II (Of Original Sin)
further_reading.says: It teaches that original sin includes real defects in human nature, among them the lack of the fear and trust of God, and that concupiscence is sin, which is not counted against believers in Christ.

further_reading.title: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, Article I (Original Sin)
further_reading.says: It teaches that original sin is the deep corruption of the whole nature, reaching the understanding, heart and will, so that the person is spiritually dead and the powers dead to what is good, while some ability remains in outward worldly matters.

further_reading.title: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, Article II (Free Will)
further_reading.says: It teaches that the unconverted person cannot prepare himself for grace or contribute to his conversion, that the Holy Spirit alone works conversion and faith through the Word and the sacraments, and that God draws the will without forcing it.

further_reading.title: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, Article XI (Election), paragraphs 28, 41 and 78
further_reading.says: It teaches that the promise of the Gospel is universal and that God is not willing that any should perish, and it gives the perverse will of man as the cause of rejecting the Word and calls unbelief the people's own fault.

further_reading.title: Luther's Small Catechism, The Creed, explanation of the Third Article
further_reading.says: It teaches that a person cannot by his own reason or strength believe in Jesus Christ or come to him, and that the Holy Spirit calls through the Gospel and keeps the believer in true faith.

further_reading.title: Martin Luther, The Bondage of the Will (1525)
further_reading.says: Luther argues that the human will, left to itself, is bound to sin and cannot turn itself toward God unless God's grace acts.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 6 (sections 2-5) and chapter 9 (section 3)
further_reading.says: Chapter 6 says the fall left people dead in sin and wholly defiled in all the parts and faculties of soul and body, and chapter 9, section 3 says man has wholly lost all ability of will to any spiritual good accompanying salvation.

further_reading.title: Canons of Dort, Third and Fourth Main Points of Doctrine, articles 1-4 and 10-12
further_reading.says: They teach that the fall corrupted every descendant of Adam, that the light of nature that remains cannot lead to saving knowledge of God, and that conversion is God's work, which renews the will so that it acts.

further_reading.title: Heidelberg Catechism, questions 3-9
further_reading.says: Question 8 teaches that people are so corrupt that they can do no good and lean toward all evil unless they are born again by the Spirit of God.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Shorter Catechism, questions 18 and 19
further_reading.says: Question 18 locates the sinfulness of the fallen estate in the guilt of Adam's first sin, the lack of original righteousness and the corruption of the whole nature, and question 19 describes its misery.

further_reading.title: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 2, chapter 1 (Through the Fall and Revolt of Adam, the Whole Human Race Made Accursed and Degenerate. Of Original Sin)
further_reading.says: Calvin argues that Adam's corruption passes to all his descendants and reaches every faculty of the soul, including the understanding and the heart.

further_reading.title: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 2, chapter 2 (Man Now Deprived of Freedom of Will, and Miserably Enslaved)
further_reading.says: Calvin argues that after the fall the will is enslaved, so that people act willingly yet cannot choose the good, and that some natural understanding remains without spiritual knowledge of God apart from the Spirit.

further_reading.title: Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion, Articles IX and X
further_reading.says: Article IX calls original sin the fault and corruption of the nature of every person and says concupiscence has of itself the nature of sin even in the baptized, and Article X says that after Adam's fall a person cannot turn and prepare himself to faith and good works without the grace of God by Christ preventing him.

further_reading.title: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church, Articles VII, VIII and XVII
further_reading.says: Article VII calls original sin a corruption of human nature inherited by everyone born of Adam, Article VIII says that after the fall no one has power to do good works pleasing to God without the grace of God by Christ preventing us, and Article XVII calls baptism a sign of regeneration or the new birth.

further_reading.title: Book of Doctrines and Discipline (2024), paragraph 102 (The Wesleyan Way of Salvation) and the Articles of Religion
further_reading.says: As reported by the readers who checked it, paragraph 102 describes prevenient grace as the first dawning of grace, awakening the conscience and restoring a measure of liberty, and places it first in a way of salvation that continues through justifying and sanctifying grace.

further_reading.title: John Wesley, Standard Sermons, Sermon 44 (Original Sin)
further_reading.says: Wesley teaches that human nature is wholly corrupted by the fall, so that every person is by nature alienated from God and needs God's renewing grace.

further_reading.title: John Wesley, Standard Sermons, Sermon 43 (The Scripture Way of Salvation), part I
further_reading.says: Wesley teaches that salvation begins with what he calls preventing grace, which includes what is commonly called natural conscience, and that the Spirit works convictions in every child of man.

further_reading.title: John Wesley, Sermon 85 (On Working Out Our Own Salvation)
further_reading.says: Wesley teaches that people are by nature spiritually dead and can do nothing good until God raises them, that no one is in a state of mere nature, and that every person has some measure of preventing grace, which comes before any human call.

further_reading.title: John Wesley, Sermon 45 (The New Birth)
further_reading.says: Wesley teaches that in time justification and the new birth coincide, and that baptism is not the new birth, which may or may not accompany it.

further_reading.title: Jacobus Arminius, Declaration of Sentiments (1608), sections III and IV
further_reading.says: Arminius writes that in his fallen state man is not capable, of and by himself, either to think, to will or to do what is really good, and that even the regenerate can do no good without preventing and following grace.

further_reading.title: The Remonstrance of 1610 (Five Articles), Article III
further_reading.says: It states that man has not saving grace of himself nor of the energy of his free will, and that he must be born again of God in Christ through the Holy Spirit.

further_reading.title: Second London (Baptist) Confession of 1689, chapter 9 (Of Free Will)
further_reading.says: Chapter 9 says man has wholly lost all ability of will to any spiritual good accompanying salvation.

further_reading.title: Assemblies of God position paper, The Assurance of Salvation (2017), section I
further_reading.says: Section I calls the grace God provides before salvation prevenient grace, enabling people either to accept or to reject his offer.

further_reading.title: Foursquare Declaration of Faith, article III
further_reading.says: Article III says that all mankind are sinners, void by nature of the holiness the law of God requires, and positively inclined to evil.

further_reading.title: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995), Article 7 (Sin), commentary
further_reading.says: It teaches that human sinfulness affects the entire person and that people's own attempts to do good and to know the truth are constantly corrupted.

further_reading.title: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995), Article 8 (Salvation), commentary
further_reading.says: It teaches that God brings people into right relationship without coercion, that the Spirit moves them to accept salvation, and that accepting it is a personal, voluntary decision.

further_reading.title: Dordrecht Confession of Faith (1632), Articles II and III
further_reading.says: Article II says sin and death spread to all people and that humans could not raise or reconcile themselves to God, and Article III speaks of their utter inability and of God's promise of reconciliation in Christ.

further_reading.title: Orthodox Church in America, Questions and Answers: Original Sin
further_reading.says: A priest's reply on the Church's teaching pages, not an adopted statement: it says that everyone bears the consequences of the first sin, the foremost of which is death, and that only Adam and Eve are guilty of it.

_why: QUOTES: every quote was read against http://localhost:8012/api/verse and ticked. Agreed: Rom 3:23, Eccl 7:20, Rom 6:23, Eph 2:8, Mark 1:15 (the last sentence of the verse). Reading 1: Gen 1:27, Gen 9:6, Jas 3:9, Rom 1:20, Rom 2:15 (clause), Luke 10:30 (the first two sentences of the verse, from 'A man was going down'; the server's opening curly quote left off), Rom 5:12, 1 Cor 15:22. Reading 2: Gen 6:5 (clause from 'every inclination'), Ps 51:5, Jer 17:9, Rom 3:11, Rom 8:7 (clause from 'the mind of the flesh'), Eph 2:1, 1 Cor 2:14, John 6:44 (without the server's opening curly quote). Reading 3: John 1:9, Tit 2:11, John 12:32 (without the closing curly quote), Rom 2:4, Acts 17:30, Deut 30:19, Isa 55:6, Phil 2:13. Verses cited only inside the answers or notes were also read on the server (Gen 8:21, Rom 2:14, Rom 8:8, Rom 9:16, Eph 2:5, Deut 30:6, Ezek 36:26, Rom 3:10 to 3:12). Refs are written in the book names of the faith-and-works card. ORDER: by when each reading was articulated, as I read the history. First the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox reading, which runs from the early church (the Western formal statements, Orange in 529 and Trent in 1546, are later than the reading they state); second the Reformation reading (from 1517, with the name 'total depravity' belonging to the Reformed five points drawn up in the early 1600s); third the Wesleyan account of prevenient grace (1700s), with the Anabaptist (1520s) and free-church positions that sit nearer it. The ordering is by history and does not rank. THREE READINGS, EIGHT PASSAGES EACH: the same count each, so no reading has more or fewer. Reading 3 and reading 2 agree that no one turns unaided; they differ on whether grace that goes before is given to all, and the card says so, so a Wesleyan or Baptist reader is not shown as denying the corruption of the person. HELD_BY: assignments are approximate and the summaries say where a tradition holds a reading in part or its members differ (Anglican in 2 and 3, because the Thirty-nine Articles speak both of a nature 'very far gone' and of grace that goes before; Baptist in 2 and 3; Lutheran and Reformed differ inside reading 2 over resistible grace; Catholic and Orthodox differ inside reading 1 over guilt). Pentecostal and Charismatic readers are placed only in 3, and a reviewer from those traditions may want to say whether some belong in 2. Nothing names a person, scholar or leader. WORDS: I checked the summaries, answers and notes for 'but', 'however', 'actually', 'clearly', 'only', 'merely'. 'And not' appears in descriptions of what a tradition teaches ('wounded and not destroyed', 'not a personal act'); it states that tradition's own contrast and is not a verdict. 'Clearly' and 'but' appear inside quotes (Rom 1:20, Rom 6:23) and are the verse's own words. Rom 3:11 is quoted alone, with the chain 3:10-12 named in the note. LEFT OUT: (a) A reading in which a person can turn to God unaided. No confession of the listed traditions teaches it (the early church and the Reformation rejected it under other names), so it is not given a place as a held reading, though some individual members of free-church and Pentecostal congregations hold something near it; a secular scholar or a Baptist reviewer may say it needs one line. (b) Jewish readings: the listed traditions are all Christian, and no Jewish tradition holds inherited sin or total depravity, so there is no reading to credit; a rabbi will note that Gen 4:7 (sin crouching at the door, 'you must master it'), Deut 30:11-14 (the commandment 'not too difficult') and Gen 8:21 (the inclination of the heart) are read in Jewish tradition as describing a capacity to choose with an inclination to resist, and the card cites Gen 6:5, Gen 8:21 and Deut 30:19 within the readings with the Christian uses named. A rabbi should say whether Gen 4:7 needs a place in reading 3. (c) Jer 13:23 ('Can the Ethiopian change his skin...') I left out on purpose: it has been used in racial readings, and the verse's point (habit of doing evil) is carried by Jer 17:9. Rom 1:28 ('a depraved mind') is also left out; 'depravity' is a word that has been turned against peoples, so the card names it as a Reformed term and says in the summary that it names the reach of sin, not that anyone is as evil as possible. A young African American believer's likely concern, that this language has been applied to some groups and not others, is why 'every person' and 'all' are the card's words throughout. (d) Pelagius and Augustine are not named (the brief bars persons); the debate is carried by the traditions' terms. (e) Election, predestination and perseverance: sibling cards. The links to those cards are not in related.cards because their ids are not yet in the entity set (free-will, election, human-nature, can-salvation-be-lost are not entities); they should be added to related.cards once they exist. (f) Rom 5:12 'because all sinned' is the Berean's rendering; the Greek clause behind it has been read in two ways (in whom all sinned, in the Latin, and because all sinned), and the two readings feed the Catholic/Orthodox difference over inherited guilt. I left the clause as the Berean has it and did not quote the Latin. (g) Ps 51:5 appears in reading 2; readers in reading 1 take it as describing a condition the psalmist shares, not a personal guilt. The answers of reading 1 do not mention it; a Catholic reviewer may want a line. (h) 2 Cor 4:4, Rom 7 and Gal 5:17 (the struggle of the flesh and the Spirit), left out for count; a Wesleyan or Pentecostal reviewer might want Rom 7 or Gal 5:17 for reading 3. (i) Pelagian-leaning free-church views and the Orthodox rejection of Augustine's account of guilt are touched in summaries only. RELATED IDS: card ids verified through /api/entity (sin, grace, faith, image_of_god, repentance, flesh, regeneration, heart, adam, conscience, death). Theme ids verified from /api/majorthemes (sin_exile_death, image_of_god, deliverance, spirit, mercy_restoration, new_creation). UNRESOLVED: the Luke 10:30 note says 'Early Christian readers took...'; a reviewer should confirm the reading is old enough to say so without naming a person. The Thirty-nine Articles are referred to only in this note, not in the card. UPDATE 2026-10-25 (cross-check): the Thirty-nine Articles are now named in the card and in further_reading; Baptist is no longer in reading 3's held_by (see _review_2026_10_25 and _for_editor); no quote was added or changed in this round.
